questions.stem: Consider this: A theorist defending a theory of law asks whether an unjust rule can still be law. The case is legally unclear but morally urgent. Which statement best states the governing legal rule on these facts?

options.text: Legal positivism treats a rule as valid when it comes from a recognized source, regardless of whether the rule is morally defensible on these facts.
Positivism holds that an unjust rule cannot be law at all on these facts.
Positivism forbids judges from ever considering moral arguments in hard cases on these facts.
options.misconception: assumes positivism denies all moral reasoning

options.text: Positivism is the claim that citizens must never resist a law they dislike on these facts.
options.misconception: treats the theory as obedience advice

questions.explanation: Positivism is a theory about the criterion of validity, not a licence for cruelty or a command to obey. It separates the question of what counts as law from the question of whether the law deserves approval. Here the decisive point is the positivist account of legal validity, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Locate the theory at the point where a rule is identified as law. Keep the inquiry on the positivist account of legal validity.
